t: LeetCode 3251 – Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs II
o: Count pairs (arr1 non-decreasing, arr2 non-increasing) with arr1[i] + arr2[i] = nums[i]. Fix arr1; arr2 is then forced. DP over positions and arr1 values: dp[i][v] = number of prefixes ending with arr1[i] = v. Transition: arr1[i-1] = u must satisfy u ≤ v and nums[i-1] − u ≥ nums[i] − v, i.e. u ≤ v − (nums[i] − nums[i-1]). So dp[i][v] = Σ_{u ≤ min(v, v−d)} dp[i-1][u] with d = nums[i] − nums[i-1]. Naively that sum is O(V) per cell; keeping running prefix sums of the previous row makes each cell O(1). With n ≤ 2000 and values ≤ 1000, the optimized version is ~2·10^6 operations.
k: Once arr1 is chosen, arr2 is determined by arr1[i] + arr2[i] = nums[i].
Transition bound: u ≤ v − (nums[i] − nums[i-1]); prefix sums collapse the O(V) inner loop to O(1).

a.n: Approach 1: Row DP with prefix sums
a.i: Keep pref[v] = Σ_{u≤v} dp[i-1][u]. Then dp[i][v] = pref[min(v, v−d)] (clamped to [0, maxVal]), rebuilt into a new prefix row each iteration. Base row: dp[0][v] = 1 for 0 ≤ v ≤ nums[0].
s: Build the base prefix row from nums[0].
For each i, compute d = nums[i] − nums[i-1]; new dp[v] = pref[w] where w = clamp(v − d if d > 0 else v).
Re-prefix the row; answer is the final row's total sum mod 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n · V) with V = max(nums) ≤ 1000 — two linear sweeps per position
a.sp: O(V) — only the previous prefix row is kept

a.i: Same state definition but compute each transition sum with an explicit inner loop over u ≤ min(v, v−d). O(n·V²) ≈ 2·10^9 — instructive but too slow; useful to validate the optimized version on small tests.
s: dp[i][v] = Σ_{u=0}^{min(v, v−d)} dp[i-1][u] mod p.
a.t: O(n · V²) — cubic in the worst case; only viable for tiny inputs

w: Always present the prefix-sum optimization — it is the intended solution and a canonical 'range-sum DP' pattern. Pitfalls: the transition cap depends on the SIGN of d (when nums decreases, the binding constraint is u ≤ v, not u ≤ v − d), clamping w into [0, V], and reducing mod 1e9+7 at every step. Sanity checks: [2,3,2] → 4, [5,5,5,5] → 126. Follow-up: count pairs where arr1 is strictly increasing (shift the transition bounds), or reconstruct one optimal pair.
